passage:
In Cape Town, Daniel's kitchen drawer was full of envelopes he hadn't opened. Most had the bank's red stripe on the front. When a new one came, he slid it under the others without looking.
"It'll sort itself out," he told Lindiwe, his flatmate, when she noticed the drawer wouldn't close. "Bonus season's coming. I'll handle it then." He said it lightly, but he switched to talking about football so fast that she stopped mid-sentence.
Last year's bonus had been smaller than promised. He knew that. He also knew that opening the envelopes would mean numbers, and numbers would mean doing something he didn't feel ready to do.
"There's a free advice centre near my work," Lindiwe said. "I could come with you." Daniel nodded at the kettle. "After payday, maybe."

qa.q: What was on the front of most of the envelopes?
qa.a: Most had the bank's red stripe on the front.

qa.q: Why does Daniel avoid opening the envelopes?
qa.a: Opening them would mean facing the numbers and having to act, which he doesn't feel ready for, so avoiding them feels safer.

qa.q: What protective step does Lindiwe offer, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She offers to go with him to a free advice centre, because qualified help and a supportive flatmate can make facing the problem less frightening.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Daniel changes the subject so fast?
qa.a: She may feel shut out and worried, since she noticed the drawer and was cut off mid-sentence.

grounding: A young man with mounting bills keeps saying it will sort itself out, because looking straight at the numbers would demand action he is not ready for.

By nine at night the office on the fourth floor was empty except for Kashish and the hum of the water cooler. It was the third late night this week. The manager had again promised that the overtime would "show in appraisals", the same line as last March.
Manjula from accounts stopped at her desk, bag on her shoulder. "You're here every night. And your salary was late in June too, na?"
"It's a phase," Kashish said. "Once the new client settles, it'll calm down." She kept her eyes on the screen.
She didn't mention the headaches, or the job alert she had deleted that morning without reading. Reading it would mean admitting this might not get better.
Manjula put a hand on the desk. "Just read one alert. That's all. Reading isn't quitting."

qa.q: What did the manager promise about the overtime?
qa.a: The manager promised the overtime would "show in appraisals", the same line as last March.

qa.q: Why did Kashish delete the job alert without reading it?
qa.a: Kashish felt afraid to read it, because reading it would mean admitting the job might not get better.

qa.q: What small step does Manjula suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Manjula suggests reading just one job alert, which lets Kashish look at the problem without having to decide everything at once.

qa.q: What might Manjula be noticing that Kashish isn't admitting?
qa.a: Manjula sees the late nights and the late salary as a pattern, and seems worried that Kashish keeps calling it a phase.

grounding: A young woman in a draining job keeps calling it a phase and avoids anything that would make her look at it straight.

passage:
Sarika, you're asking about work again. It's fine. Seriously. Okay, the salary was late in July, and August, and this month it's the fifteenth and nothing yet. But the owner said funding is coming. He's a good guy. Nilesh, he told me, you're my most trusted person. That means something, right?
And yes, three people left. And yes, they don't answer my messages about whether they got their dues. But they were negative people.
Honestly, if I start job-hunting now, what does that say? That I gave up. That I chose wrong in the first place. My parents told everyone I work at a "startup." I can't come home and say it's falling apart.
It'll sort itself out. These things do.
…
Why are you looking at me like that? Fine. Maybe I don't want to look at it. Maybe if I look at it, I have to do something.

qa.q: Which months was Nilesh's salary late?
qa.a: The salary was late in July, and August, and this month it's the fifteenth and nothing yet.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh keep saying "It'll sort itself out"?
qa.a: Nilesh feels afraid and ashamed of admitting a wrong choice and disappointing the family, so avoiding the signs feels safer than acting.

qa.q: What would you advise Nilesh to do next?
qa.a: List the warning signs honestly with Sarika, speak to a trusted mentor or a qualified adviser about the unpaid salary, and quietly start looking at other jobs.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel listening to Nilesh?
qa.a: Sarika is probably worried for Nilesh, which shows in the look that finally makes Nilesh admit he's avoiding the truth.

grounding: It shows a young adult ignoring clear warning signs at work and insisting it will sort itself out because facing it would demand action.

passage:
March. Thomas checked Charu's phone while she was in the shower. When she came out, he asked who "Rahul office" was. She laughed it off. He's just protective, she thought.
April. Charu cancelled dinner with her college friends for the third time because Thomas sulked all evening when she went out. "It's easier to stay home," she told herself. "He's stressed about his exams. It'll settle after June."
May. Her friend Meenal texted: "Haven't seen you in two months. You okay? Honestly?" Charu looked at the message for a long time. Her thumb hovered. She typed, "All good! Just busy," and deleted it. She typed it again. Thomas walked in, and she put the phone face down, heart racing.
Later that night, after he slept, she opened Meenal's message again and wrote: "Not really. Can we talk tomorrow?"

qa.q: Who did Thomas ask about after checking Charu's phone?
qa.a: He asked who "Rahul office" was.

qa.q: What does Charu's heart racing when Thomas walks in suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Charu feels afraid and tense, even while she keeps telling herself everything will settle after June.

qa.q: What small step at the end could help Charu?
qa.a: Replying honestly to Meenal and meeting her the next day lets a trusted friend help her look clearly at what is happening, and perhaps find a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Meenal see the last two months?
qa.a: Meenal is worried, noticing that her friend has disappeared from their life, which is why she asks "Honestly?"

grounding: It shows a young adult explaining away warning signs in a relationship over months because facing them would demand action.

passage:
Chinmay, let your Santosh Uncle tell you about the drawer.
When I was twenty-five, I borrowed a little from a friend, then a little from a card, then a little more to pay the first two. Each time, I said, "Next month it'll all come right." Letters from the bank came, and I didn't open them. I put them in the bottom drawer of my desk. The drawer got fuller. I stopped opening the drawer.
If I didn't look, I didn't have to do anything. And I was not ready to do anything.
One Sunday your aunt was looking for a pen and opened that drawer. She didn't shout. She sat on the floor, opened every envelope, and put them in order by date. Then she said, "Tomorrow we go and talk to someone who knows about this." We went to a proper advisor at the bank.
It took years. But it started with opening the drawer.

qa.q: Where did Santosh put the letters from the bank?
qa.a: He put them in the bottom drawer of his desk.

qa.q: How did young Santosh feel about the drawer?
qa.a: He felt afraid and overwhelmed, so avoiding the drawer let him escape the action he was not ready to take.

qa.q: What turning point in the story began the real change?
qa.a: When his wife opened the envelopes in order and they went to a proper advisor at the bank the next day.

qa.q: How might Santosh's wife have felt when she found the drawer?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and worried, but she stayed calm and chose to help rather than shout.

grounding: An uncle recalls ignoring a growing debt pattern by hiding unopened letters, and the day the family finally looked at it together.

passage:
The electricity bill arrived the same morning as the third reminder from the credit card company, and Siddharth put both, unopened, under the fruit bowl. Rent was due in four days. His salary was due in six.
It'll sort itself out, he told himself. Next month's bonus. Or the side project. He had been saying it since March.
His phone buzzed with an unknown number. He turned it face down.
At lunch his sister Sunaina called. "You sound tired. Everything okay?"
"All good. Just busy." He laughed. He always laughed.
That night he couldn't sleep. At 2 am he lifted the fruit bowl and looked at the envelopes, then put the bowl back on top. Opening them would mean knowing the number. Knowing the number would mean doing something.
He lay in the dark, heart racing, telling himself one more time that it would all work out.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth put the envelopes?
qa.a: Under the fruit bowl, unopened.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth put the fruit bowl back on the envelopes at 2 am?
qa.a: Siddharth felt frightened; opening them would mean knowing the number and having to act, which he wasn't ready for.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do instead of waiting for it to sort itself out?
qa.a: Open the envelopes in daylight, tell Sunaina the truth when she calls, and speak to a qualified debt adviser about the options.

qa.q: What would change if Sunaina knew what was under the fruit bowl?
qa.a: Sunaina could offer support and help him find proper advice, instead of hearing 'all good' while he lies awake.

grounding: Shows an adult with mounting bills telling himself it will sort itself out, because looking straight at it would demand action.
